content_voiceover: Now we move to neuroblastoma, the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood. It arises from neural crest cells of the sympathoadrenal lineage. Pathologically there is a maturation spectrum, from neuroblastoma, to ganglioneuroblastoma, to the fully mature and benign ganglioneuroma. Hereditary neuroblastoma is linked to mutations in PHOX2B and ALK. For workup, look for elevated urinary catecholamine metabolites, homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid, with VMA greater than seven milligrams per day being significant, along with functional imaging using F-eighteen FDOPA PET or I-one-two-three MIBG scan. Prognostic factors are numerous, staging system, which has evolved from the older Evans system, to INSS, to the current INRG system, age at diagnosis with a cutoff that has shifted from one year to one point five years, Shimada histology, degree of differentiation, MYCN amplification which predicts advanced disease and treatment failure, and chromosomal changes, where one p deletion, eleven q deletion, and seventeen q gain in a diploid tumor are unfavorable, while hyperdiploidy is more favorable. Treatment ranges widely by risk group, from observation alone in low-risk infants, to chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy, and thirteen-cis-retinoic acid, up to autologous stem cell transplant plus anti-GD2 immunotherapy for high-risk disease.
keypoints: Neural crest origin, maturation spectrum from neuroblastoma to ganglioneuroma
Hereditary neuroblastoma linked to PHOX2B and ALK mutations
Elevated urinary HVA and VMA, plus MIBG scan or FDOPA PET for workup
MYCN amplification and eleven q deletion predict advanced disease and worse outcome
High-risk treatment includes autologous stem cell transplant and anti-GD2 immunotherapy
keypoint_voiceover: Neuroblastoma spans a maturation spectrum from malignant neuroblastoma to benign ganglioneuroma. For workup, remember urinary HVA and VMA plus MIBG scan. For prognosis, MYCN amplification and eleven q deletion are the red flags for aggressive disease, while hyperdiploidy is reassuring. And for treatment, low risk may just need observation, but high-risk disease escalates all the way to autologous transplant combined with anti-GD2 immunotherapy.
